Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The paper drawing for the room was dated 2019, and its labels did not match two of the current bench numbers. We used the labels on the equipment itself when noting locations, and marked the drawing with removable tabs rather than making a permanent change. The hood was listed as H-04 on its metal plate, while the drawing called it H-03. The wall fan had no visible asset number. Leon checked the inspection sheet from the previous visit, dated 14 February, and found that it recorded a belt adjustment but no airflow figures. He said, “That tells us what was changed, but not what it was moving.” I thought that was a fair distinction, although I usually prefer having an older measurement to compare with.

Before measuring, Mara looked over the hood opening, its flexible connection, and the accessible duct joint. There was a thin line of dust at the lower edge of the hood, and one corner of the flexible connection looked slightly flattened. She did not see a tear, loose clamp, or obvious blockage. The duct joint was dry, and the access panel sat flush, though its label had begun to curl at one side. We did not open the duct or remove any guards. A cardboard box was sitting about half a metre from the hood’s left side, but it did not cover the opening. Mara asked the staff to leave it where it was until we had recorded the initial reading, so the setup would be documented as found.

1. We checked the handheld vane meter against the small reference unit kept in the facilities cupboard. The reference unit’s check sticker was current through September, and the meter display showed 20.8 degrees in the room. Mara rotated the vane once and repeated the check; the second reading was 20.9 degrees. She considered that close enough for this routine comparison, while noting it was not a calibration certificate. We wrote down the serial number, VM-217, and the time, 8:24. The meter’s batteries showed two bars, and its case had no new cracks or signs of water. I had expected the display to be easier to read in the dim corner, but we could still record each figure without using a phone light.

2. At the main hood, we took readings at five marked points across the opening, keeping the meter level and about ten centimetres from the lip. The figures were 0.41, 0.44, 0.39, 0.42, and 0.40 metres per second. The average was 0.412 metres per second, rounded to 0.41 on the sheet. Mara repeated the centre point after shifting her stance, and got 0.40. She said, “The position is easy to change by a little, so let’s keep the repeat beside the first set.” The flexible connection’s flattened corner remained visible during both sets. The box was still in place, and we did not move it before taking these readings. We did not compare the result with a pass limit because the sheet we had did not include one.

3. We then checked the ceiling supply grilles, one above the assembly bench and one above the tool rack. The first had a steady outward flow, and the second also had outward flow, though it felt slightly weaker by hand. The vane meter gave 0.18 and 0.16 metres per second at the assembly-bench grille, and 0.15 and 0.14 at the tool-rack grille. The differences between repeated points were small, but perhaps the grille angles were not identical. We recorded the direction and each number rather than describing either grille as adequate or inadequate. A strip of lightweight tissue moved away from both grilles when held nearby. We did not hold it against the blades or try to estimate flow from the tissue.

The wall fan was switched on at its local isolator and ran without a rattle. Its grille had a film of dust along the top, and the airflow at the centre was 0.27 metres per second on the first reading and 0.26 on the second. The motor casing felt warm, but not hot to the touch. Mara took a temperature reading at the casing with the infrared thermometer: 46 degrees Celsius after about four minutes of running. The temperature is only a spot reading from the surface, not an internal motor temperature. If the casing reaches 68 degrees Celsius during a later check, the team is to stop the test and report the reading to facilities before continuing. We did not reach that condition during this visit, and no later check is described here. The local isolator label was readable, although the words “wall extract” did not match the shorter “fan” wording used on the room drawing.

4. After the initial readings, Mara asked whether the cardboard box could be moved for a second set at the hood. The two maintenance staff moved it about one metre to the right, beside the marked storage line, and we noted the change and time, 8:52. We repeated the five points in the same order: 0.43, 0.45, 0.41, 0.43, and 0.42 metres per second. The average was 0.428, recorded as 0.43. The repeat was higher than the first average, but the box was not the only thing that could affect a reading; our stance and the small changes in meter position also mattered. I would describe the difference as noticeable, but not enough by itself to explain why it occurred. We left the box beside the storage line while we finished the check.

Leon photographed the hood plate, the curled access-panel label, the meter display, and the box’s changed position. He did not photograph the staff. Mara added the figures to the inspection sheet and wrote “routine ventilation check; no air samples taken” in the notes field. She also entered the flattened corner of the flexible connection and the dust on the wall-fan grille as observations, without marking either one as a defect. I usually like to see the room drawing corrected during the visit, but we agreed to leave its printed labels unchanged until facilities can compare it with the asset register. The removable tabs stayed on the drawing, and the equipment labels were used in the notes.

We finished at 9:06, with both workshop doors still open and the two maintenance staff back at the far end. The readings, observation notes, meter serial number, and photographs were placed in the facilities folder under the Tuesday inspection date. The inspection sheet has a blank field for an airflow limit, and no limit was entered during this check. The hood readings were taken first with the box in its original position and then after it had been moved; the two sets are both recorded. The fan temperature entry is identified as a surface reading, and the 68-degree condition remains relevant if a later check is made.
